President's Investment Drive

By: Siniketiwe Hlanze | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We take stock of the president's various investment efforts to unlock the country's sluggish economy.

Unique Selling Point:
With the country's economy only set to grow by less than 1 percent this year, a disastrous unemployment rate for a developing economy and international monetary bodies raising red flags at the slow pace of reforms, with much optimism President Cyril Ramaphosa tells the world that South Africa is open for business. An interview with one of the presidential envoys instructed to sell the country to potential investors ( Phumzile Langeni or Jaco Maree), talk to the association of car global manufacturers which made a pledge of R6bn at the 2019 summit (Tim Abbot)
South African Chamber of Commerce and Industry is local business behind these investment drives and lastly Gina Schoeman Investment Economist at Citi Bank to make all of this make sense.

Summary:
The piece will essentially address two main questions, how does the country with a stagnant economy attract investment and is investment be it FDI or local the key we need to unlock economic growth. Sentiment and perception are big drivers of investment and as the country battles load shedding and goes through slow implementation of economic reform pursuing ambitious investment efforts seems to be pie in the sky solutions for serious challenges.

Further information:
Treatment; an economic story driven by interviews with newsmakers, business magazine content but water cooler conversation vocabulary.

Tim Abbot BMW CEO
Alan Mukoki SACCI CEO
Jacko Maree Presidential Envoy

Press Release:


The President’s Investment Drive
With the economy set to grow by less than one percent this year and international monetary bodies warning against the slow pace of reforms, why is President Cyril Ramaphosa saying that South Africa is open for business? After two years of presidential envoys trotting the globe to woo investors, we take stock of the returns on the president’s investment drive and ask where the hope for South Africa’s sluggish economy will come from.
Producer: Siniketiwe Hlanze | Presenter: Masa Kekana


Script:



President Cyril Ramaphosa has been courting investors both local and international.
CYRIL SONA: 1:00:38. We will hold our third annual investment conference in November to review the implementation of previous commitments and to generate new investment in our economy


CYRIL RAMAPHOSA – INVESTMENT SUMMIT

The flagship investment summits were announced with a goal to raise R1.2 trillion worth of investments.Here businesses financially endorse the president’s economic vision.



Mike Mabasa is CEO of the National Auto-motive Association of South Africa – which represents the business interests of global car manufacturers operating in the country.






MIKE: 0:40 The automotive industry is important to South Africa because we contribute 30 percent of the entire manufacturing output. So 30 percent of everything that is manufactured in south Africa 30 percent of that comes from that sector, so there’s no way that we can not invest, so when the president put out the call to the entire private sector to invest, we saw this as an opportunity for us to raise our hands and to contribute meaningfully to the economy of the country.



Masa – First question
Mike: so the money mainly goes into our capital expenditure, so we invest into our manufacting lines, our members will come up with their plans to say in the next 5 years to renew a model or to update a particular model. In order to do that successfully you say. So it’s capital expenditure firstly, secondly it’s obviously people eh our technology is changing everyday, the car brain, so you need to be able to make sure that people are trained

LINK: Government has concentrated its efforts to attracting investments into the country in order to kickstart the economy, with growth expected at just less than 1 percent this year, is this the right strategy to turn things around.



Jacko: If you think about it there not many levers to pull

Investment Envoy Jacko Maree is one of four people appointed by the president to travel the world and present the country’s commercial opportunities to big companies and conglomerates.



Jacko: Government didnt’ have money….etc

Economist at Citi Bank, Gina Schoeman says coupled with other strategies, foreign direct investment, could have a knock on effect for the growth we desperately need





08:41 Gina – the solution is to start at home, if you want to attract FDI, if you want to attract any type of investment you have to clean up your shop, you have to show off your talent and skills because that’s the incentive to draw the investment in. now ask yourself we have talents and skills in South Africa but we can’t see them at the moment because we’re not getting down to the nitty gritty which is energy, which is loadshedding, which is fiscal risk, which is the downgrades, which is all off that is linked together, we’re not getting down to structural reforms, structural reform is what is necessary to grow the country’s economy to give it an economic future and that’s something that investors get excited about because it’s going to give them a return on investment

Although making a very significant contribution to the president’s investment efforts, local business confidence is beginning to dwindle.
South African Chamber of Commerce and Industry CEO, Alan Mukoki, says the private sector would like to see more concrete effort to attract investment




Alan: at a global level I think we are making the right noises, driving the right narrative about South Africa is a good investment destination but we need to have things that we’re selling to the people that are really interesting to the people who have the money and can bring projects to South Africa
Masa: 7:50 Ahhlan are you saying we aren’t seeing tangible results from the summits
Alan: What I’m saying is that if I’m sitting in London or Tokyo... We are not there yet where we are able to articulate, you have to be able to sell something to South Africa, you can’t be selling a dream


Whilst the country’s investment potential is widely promoted, the difficult task is getting a buy-in from keen investors



Masa question: During her visit here, German Chancelor Angela Merkel said, German Businesses want to do business with South Africa but they want good conditions and less bureaucracy, can we promise such countries such things.

Jacko- I think you’ve seen a number of areas in recent times where you have seen policy unloks



Loadshedding, we may be Africa’s most industrialized economy but our lack of energy is threatening the sectors that could bring in a much needed economic injection.
Masa Walking Link:
After two summits, the president has passed the half-way mark of his R1.2 trillion investment target. Our strong banking systems and developed infrastructure are our drawcard to the world - but without implementations of reforms and economic growth can we attract new investors
Masa03:00: When investors hear South Africa, do they think that’s where I want to put my money
03:04Gina - I guess it depends on what type of investor you are if you’re talking about international, off shore investor, actual capex so coming to South Africa to build new things, it would be very important as to how the economy is doing. So I’ve always said that naturally when you’re looking for FDI …03:54 If it’s an off shore foreign investor who is looking to bring business to South Africa or expand current business in South Africa, well of course the political climate, the economic climate, the certainty about the future that really comes into play




3:56 Masa: When you speak to the companies that you represent, your bmws, mercedes benz - how do alleviate their concerns when the reality is there are no lights
Mike: Well it’s a difficult conversation and many of them have , these are global brands and a bmw here in rosalin SOuth Africa...so a BMW head office in Munich when they make decisions about where to invest in the future, they look at the matrix in order to say where are the safe markets , where they can for an example secure a stable supply of energy, where there are no issues and concerns around labour and so competitiveness in our business is very important, so if we are not competitive as South Africa, certainly we are going to see a lot of these players moving their plants from South Africa, eg general motors
LINK:
Factories, jobs and new products and services, these are some of the offshoots from the investment summits. Plausible achievements, however the president’s economic legacy will also include an all-time high unemployment rate, load shedding and a constraining fiscal debt

Masa: Mike will we see your members invest in 202

Mike Absolutely



PROMO1: As the economy trudges through turbulent waters when will the country start seeing the returns from president Cyril Ramaphosa’s various investment drives.

PROMO2: Jobs and infrastructure development are some of the achievements touted from the President’s investment summits however these are overshadowed by the realities of a sluggish economy
PROMO 3: Masa: Are you saying we’re not seeing concrete details coming from the investment summit - Alan: You can’t be selling a dream or a hope
